content:
The unemployment rate doesn’t count everyone without a job.

Its denominator is the number of employed people plus the number of unemployed people. Whether someone is counted as unemployed depends on more than whether they currently have a job.

Generally, they must not have been employed during the survey’s reference week, must have been available for work (with temporary illness as an exception), and must have actively searched for work during the four weeks ending with that week.

There’s an exception to the search requirement: someone on temporary layoff who expects to be recalled may qualify without actively searching, as long as they meet the other conditions. But if someone’s only job-search activity was browsing listings, that alone doesn’t meet the active-search requirement.

Those distinctions determine who is counted as unemployed—and included in the rate’s denominator.
